subtopics.title: Perfect Competition — Assumptions, and the Industry Against the Business

questions.question: Which list gives assumptions of perfect competition?
options: Very many small buyers and sellers, a homogeneous product, free entry and exit, perfect knowledge, mobile factors
One seller, unique product, blocked entry
A few large sellers, branded products, heavy advertising
Government-set prices and licensed sellers

questions.question: The individual business in perfect competition is a PRICE TAKER, meaning:
options: It sets whatever price maximises profit
It accepts the price set by industry demand and supply, and decides only its quantity
It negotiates prices with each customer
It always charges below the market price

questions.question: The demand curve facing the individual business is:
options: Downward sloping like the industry curve
Vertical at the chosen output
A horizontal line at the market price — it can sell any quantity at that price and nothing above it
Upward sloping

questions.question: In perfect competition, the flat line at the market price is simultaneously:
options: Total cost, total revenue and profit
The industry demand and supply curves
Marginal cost, average cost and average variable cost
The demand curve, average revenue and marginal revenue — D equals AR equals MR equals P

subtopics.title: Costs, Revenue and the Profit-Maximising Output

questions.question: The marginal cost curve cuts the average cost curve:
options: At AC's lowest point — while the marginal unit costs less than the average it drags the average down; once it costs more, it pulls the average up
At AC's highest point
Never — the curves are parallel
Only when the firm makes a loss

questions.question: The universal profit-maximising rule is to produce where:
options: Average cost is at its minimum
Marginal revenue equals marginal cost, with MC rising
Total revenue is at its maximum
Price equals average variable cost

questions.question: NORMAL profit is:
options: Zero earnings
Any profit reported to SARS
The minimum earnings needed to keep the entrepreneur in the industry — an opportunity cost already included in the cost curves
Profit above all costs

questions.question: Price is R15, average cost at the best output is R12, and output is 200 units. Economic profit is:
options: Zero — this is normal profit
R600 — the R3 per-unit surplus times 200 units, the rectangle between the price line and the AC curve

subtopics.title: Losses, the Shut-Down Decision, and the Long Run

questions.question: A loss-making firm should keep producing in the short run when:
options: Price covers average variable cost — each unit then contributes something toward the fixed costs owed anyway
Price is below average variable cost
Fixed costs are zero
The owner is an optimist

questions.question: The firm's short-run supply curve is:
options: The whole average cost curve
Its rising marginal cost curve above minimum average variable cost
The horizontal price line
The industry demand curve

questions.question: When firms in the industry earn economic profit, the long-run sequence is:
options: Firms exit, supply falls, price rises
The government caps the price
Newcomers enter, industry supply shifts right, price falls until it touches minimum average cost and economic profit disappears
Nothing changes because profit is permanent

questions.question: Long-run equilibrium in perfect competition achieves both efficiencies because:
options: Firms advertise heavily
Output is restricted below demand
The state sets prices at cost
Price equals marginal cost (allocative efficiency) and output occurs at minimum average cost (productive efficiency)

subtopics.title: Competition Policy — Pushing Real Markets Toward the Benchmark

questions.question: The three institutions of the Competition Act 1998, in order of function, are:
options: The Commission investigates, the Tribunal adjudicates, and the Competition Appeal Court hears appeals
The Reserve Bank, the Treasury and SARS
The Tribunal investigates, the Commission fines, the High Court appeals
The JSE, the FSCA and the Ombudsman

questions.question: The bread cartel and the World Cup construction cases are examples of:
options: Legal vertical integration
Horizontal restrictive practices — collusion between rivals through price fixing and bid rigging
Merger control
Public-interest conditions

questions.question: South African merger control is distinctive because it also weighs:
options: The nationality of the CEO
Only shareholder returns
Public interest — employment, small-business access and the spread of ownership
The firms' advertising budgets

questions.question: In terms of the model, collusion is attacked because it:
options: Lowers prices below cost
Increases the number of sellers
Guarantees productive efficiency
Converts many competing price takers into one price maker — output restricted, price above marginal cost, the efficiencies lost

questions.question: Charging R12 when the street price is R10 fails because:
options: Buyers step two tables over and buy identical tomatoes for R10
It is against municipal by-laws
Tomatoes spoil at higher prices
The other sellers report her

questions.question: Cutting to R8 is foolish because:
options: Buyers distrust cheap tomatoes
She could already sell everything she brought at R10 — she throws away R2 on every kilo
The other sellers will match R8
Selling fast is bad for business

questions.question: The seller's only real decision on the street is:
options: What price to charge
What brand name to use
How many kilos to bring — quantity, because the street sets the price
Which buyers to refuse

questions.question: "Each wall keeps the price honest" refers to:
options: The municipal fences around the market
The tables the sellers use
Rising marginal costs
The assumptions — many sellers, identical goods, visible prices, free entry — whose removal would give a seller price power

subtopics.title: How Many Kilos? — the One Rule

questions.question: The cost of one more kilo rises as she brings more because:
options: Beyond her own garden she must buy from neighbours at rising prices, hire a bakkie and pay her cousin
Tomato prices fall in the afternoon
The municipality taxes big sellers
Buyers demand discounts for bulk

questions.question: The street version of MR equals MC is:
options: Bring as many kilos as the bakkie holds
Keep adding kilos while one more earns more than it costs; stop when the next kilo would cost more than it earns
Stop when total cost equals total revenue
Sell until noon and then go home

questions.question: Her own forgone factory wage belongs in the costs because:
options: SARS requires it
It reduces her selling price
A morning at the table is a morning's wages lost — opportunity cost, which is why normal profit sits inside the cost curves
The factory pays her anyway

questions.question: All-in cost R10 per kilo, street price R10. The verdict is:
options: Economic loss — she should quit today
Economic profit of R10 per kilo
She cannot cover her variable costs
Normal profit — she earns exactly what her time and money could earn anywhere, and staying makes sense

questions.question: "Profit was the invitation; entry was the RSVP" describes:
options: Economic profit attracting newcomers through free entry until extra supply pushes the price down and the surplus disappears
A government subsidy scheme
Sellers inviting buyers to the market
The shut-down decision

questions.question: In the drought year, losses lead to:
options: More tables joining the street
Exit — some sellers quit, supply falls, price climbs until the survivors break even
A permanent price ceiling
The street closing forever

questions.question: The street's resting point, in model language, is:
options: Price above marginal cost with restricted output
Maximum revenue for every seller
Price equal to marginal cost and to minimum average cost — normal profit only, both efficiencies achieved
Zero sellers and zero buyers

questions.question: The Sunday meeting where forty sellers agree on a R15 floor is:
options: Sound business practice
Legal if the price is fair
Merger control
Illegal collusion — price fixing that the Commission investigates and the Tribunal can fine at up to ten percent of turnover
